title: What the century teaches
hookLine: faith, courage and shared food carried a small people through

lines: FLOUR, SALT, A BUNDLE OF PRAYERS.
cards: A saddlebag. Leather, worn soft, small enough to sling behind a rider. Open one from the hard century and what's inside?
Some flour, maybe. A little salt. A wrapped bundle of prayers in Gurmukhi.

In the stories, beside a horse and a weapon, that's close to everything a hunted rider owned. Yet the people who carried bags like that came through the century, still a people, still praying, still feeding strangers.

teach.b: Sikhs sum up Guru Nanak's teaching in three short phrases: naam japo, remember the Name; kirat karo, earn honestly; vand chhako, share what you have.
Hold them up against the hard century and you'll find them there, with courage standing beside them. First, the Name.
The riders said the morning prayers from memory, opened the Granth wherever they stopped, and sang Kirtan Sohila in camps without lamps. The Ardas ties rising spirits to the Name.

teach.h: FAITH: THE NAME COULD NOT BE TAKEN.
teach.b: When everything else could be taken, the Name couldn't.
Second, courage, but not the courage of revenge. The Ardas remembers the martyrs by what they endured and names no enemy.
The courage the century hands on stands, shields the families, rebuilds at the ruins, and answers the door after dark. Third, honest bread, shared.
Guru Nanak, in the Guru Granth Sahib, says in paraphrase that one who earns by work and gives some of it with their own hands has recognized the way. That's kirat and vand in one line.

teach.h: SHARED FOOD: THE POT BEFORE THE SWORD.
teach.b: The Khalsa put the cooking pot before the sword, kept a common pot in the forests, and fed whoever came to the fire. So the saddlebag holds a Name, a backbone, a pot. None of them is heavy.
All of them can be shared. None needed a building, a treasury or a government. And it doesn't take a war to apply.
On an ordinary Tuesday, the question is the one the riders lived: what carries you?

how: Sikhs teach Guru Nanak's way as naam japo, kirat karo and vand chhako, remembering the Name, honest work and sharing, and they tell the stories of the hard century as that way lived under pressure.

o: share what you have with others
a fast kept on holy days
keep what you earn for your own family

games.q: what was in the saddlebag — tap the pairs.

s: the century's lesson is that the strongest army wins
what carried the Sikhs was the Name, courage without revenge, and shared food.
Guru Nanak says the one who earns by work and shares has recognized the way
it's in the Guru Granth Sahib, and it's the root of vand chhako.
the three things that carried them needed buildings and a treasury
none of them did. the Name, courage and a common pot all fit in a saddlebag.

games.q: you can take only three things into the hunted years. which set does the century's story say carried the Sikhs through?
o: gold, walls and a strong ally.
the Name, courage that stands, and a shared pot.
games.why: the stories keep returning to the same three: prayer from memory, courage without revenge, and food shared with whoever came.

practice: Ask yourself: when things got hard, what actually got me through, not what should have?
Let a few things come, a practice, a person, a phrase, a stubbornness you're quietly proud of, then choose three and name each one silently, as if laying them on a blanket before a long ride.
If you pray, close with Waheguru on a slow breath out.

wordCard.voice: vand chhako, share what you have. Alongside faith in the Name and courage without revenge, this carried a small people through the century. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for vand chhako, share what you have, one of the three phrases that sum up Guru Nanak's way.

carryVoice: Your line: what carries you. A Name, a backbone, a pot. That's day eight hundred eighty-five.
